excerpt: A traffic ticket carries weight with adjusters but rarely reaches a jury and never settles fault. How citations and guilty pleas are used in Georgia and South Carolina, and when negligence per se applies.
keyTakeaways: Traffic tickets carry weight with insurance adjusters but are not conclusive, and the ticket itself is generally not admissible at trial in Georgia or South Carolina. The doctrine of negligence per se may apply when a traffic violation directly causes an accident. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina use modified comparative fault, allowing recovery even with shared fault. Pleading guilty to a traffic ticket can be used against you in a civil case. Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina has 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Does a traffic ticket automatically determine fault in a car accident?
faqs.answer: No. A traffic ticket carries weight with insurance adjusters but is not conclusive, and in Georgia and South Carolina the ticket itself is generally not admissible at trial. Fault in a civil injury claim is determined by the legal system based on all available evidence, not by the police citation. The officer may not have witnessed the accident and could have incomplete information.

faqs.question: Can I still file a claim if I received a traffic ticket?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under comparative fault rules in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina, you can recover damages even if you share some fault. If you were 20% at fault due to a traffic violation, you can still recover 80% of your damages. Only reaching the state threshold (50% in GA, 51% in SC) bars recovery.

faqs.question: What is negligence per se and how does it relate to traffic tickets?
faqs.answer: Negligence per se is a legal doctrine under which violating a safety statute — such as a traffic law — establishes that the driver breached a duty of care, so the injured person does not have to prove separately that the driver acted unreasonably. It applies only when the injured person is within the group the statute protects and the harm is the kind it was meant to prevent, and the violation must still be shown to be the proximate cause of the accident. Running a red light that caused a collision supports negligence per se; a broken taillight in a head-on collision does not.

faqs.question: Should I fight a traffic ticket after a car accident?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Pleading guilty to a traffic violation can be used as an admission of fault in your civil injury case, and in Georgia posting a cash bond and skipping court is treated the same way (O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58). A dismissal, or a plea of nolo contendere where the court allows one, keeps that admission out. Consult your personal injury attorney before making any decisions in traffic court, as the two cases are strategically linked.

faqs.question: What happens if no ticket was issued at the accident scene?
faqs.answer: The absence of a traffic citation does not mean no one was at fault. Your claim can rely on other evidence including witness statements, surveillance footage, accident reconstruction analysis, cell phone records, and vehicle black box data to establish the other driver's negligence.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a car accident claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Do not delay filing because of uncertainty about traffic tickets — consult an attorney promptly.
